r: でもできるようになった。
p.e: Nowadays you can do almost anything with a phone alone.
If you lose your way the map tells you, and a word you do not know can be looked up on the spot.
Whether a shop is busy, and whether a train is late, you can know as you walk.

r: ったものもあるのではないか。
p.e: But I wonder whether, to the extent that life has become convenient, something has also been lost.
Before, you would ask someone the way to the station.
You looked at their face and thanked them.
Now there is no need for that.
Walk while looking at the screen and you arrive at your destination.
It has become quicker, but there is no contact with another person in it.

r: ませることも、めずらしくなくなった。
p.e: Getting a day's errands done without speaking to anyone has stopped being unusual.
What made me notice this was a trip with my grandmother.
My grandmother does not carry a phone.
When she does not know the way, she goes into a nearby shop and asks.

r: をすすめてくれたりする。
p.e: The shopkeeper then tells her a short cut that is not on the map, or recommends somewhere cheap and good.
It was far richer than the information I had got by looking things up.
On the second day we took a road a shopkeeper had told us about and came out at a square where a festival was being set up.
On a trip made by looking things up, I do not think we would ever have gone that way.
There is one more thing I noticed.

r: えようとしなくなったことだ。
p.e: That I have stopped trying to remember things.
Before, I naturally remembered the telephone numbers of shops I often went to and the names of the stations where I changed trains.
Now they are all inside the phone.
Since they come up when they are needed, there is no reason to keep them in my head.
But it is certainly true that the town felt more like my own town back when I remembered it.
Of course I do not mean to make convenience the villain.
For someone carrying heavy bags, or with a small child in tow, being able to look something up and move at once is a help.
I also know the reassurance of having a map in your hand on an unfamiliar road at night.

r: めているかどうかだろう。
p.e: The problem is not the tool, but whether you decide for yourself how much to leave to it.
There is no need to throw the convenient tool away.

r: としてしまうのかもしれない。
p.e: But if you come to rely on it entirely, you may overlook what you could in fact have had.
The small trouble of asking brings a short conversation with a stranger along with it.
It is that conversation, I think, that makes a trip a trip.

en:

But I wonder whether, to the extent that life has become convenient, something has also been lost.
Before, you would ask someone the way to the station. You looked at their face and thanked them. Now there is no need for that. Walk while looking at the screen and you arrive at your destination. It has become quicker, but there is no contact with another person in it. Getting a day's errands done without speaking to anyone has stopped being unusual.
What made me notice this was a trip with my grandmother. My grandmother does not carry a phone. When she does not know the way, she goes into a nearby shop and asks. The shopkeeper then tells her a short cut that is not on the map, or recommends somewhere cheap and good. It was far richer than the information I had got by looking things up. On the second day we took a road a shopkeeper had told us about and came out at a square where a festival was being set up. On a trip made by looking things up, I do not think we would ever have gone that way.
There is one more thing I noticed. That I have stopped trying to remember things. Before, I naturally remembered the telephone numbers of shops I often went to and the names of the stations where I changed trains. Now they are all inside the phone. Since they come up when they are needed, there is no reason to keep them in my head. But it is certainly true that the town felt more like my own town back when I remembered it.
Of course I do not mean to make convenience the villain. For someone carrying heavy bags, or with a small child in tow, being able to look something up and move at once is a help. I also know the reassurance of having a map in your hand on an unfamiliar road at night. The problem is not the tool, but whether you decide for yourself how much to leave to it.
There is no need to throw the convenient tool away. But if you come to rely on it entirely, you may overlook what you could in fact have had. The small trouble of asking brings a short conversation with a stranger along with it. It is that conversation, I think, that makes a trip a trip.

p.e: As a child, I was afraid of failing.

In terms of marks, that approach was not a bad one.
But what I did not understand stayed not understood.
After I started working, that view changed.

r: しながら、しんちょうに
p.e: When I was given a new job, I went about it carefully, checking over and over so as never to fail once.
I made a detailed plan and wrote out every problem that seemed likely to arise.

r: したほどよくなかった。
p.e: But the result was not as good as I had hoped.

r: いていないものだった。
p.e: Of the problems I had written out, two actually happened, and most of the problems that happened were ones I had not written.

r: は、わたしとはちがった。
p.e: The colleague at the next desk, who joined when I did, was different from me.
She tried things as soon as she thought of them, and changed her approach the moment she saw it was not working.
She built something small, showed it to people, and fixed what they told her the same day.
She failed far more often than I did, but in the end she produced a good result.

r: はどこにあったのだろう。
p.e: Where did that difference lie?
I thought of failure as something to avoid; she thought of it as something to find early.
Trying to avoid it means trying fewer things.
And if you do not try things, you cannot even tell what you do not understand.
In the end, what I had been doing was going on being safely wrong at my desk.
I have changed how I work a little since.
First I break the work into pieces small enough that a failure can be recovered from.
Within a piece that size, when in doubt I choose to try it.
I keep a short record of what I tried and read it back just once a week.

r: つまずいていたら、それは
p.e: If I have tripped twice for the same reason, I take that to be a problem with my method rather than with luck.

r: せばよいわけではない。

r: かすかなのだと、そのとき

r: ちのよいことではない。
p.e: Even now, being wrong is not a pleasant thing.
But the time the embarrassment lasts has grown much shorter than it used to be.

en:
As a child, I was afraid of failing. It was because raising my hand and getting the answer wrong was embarrassing. So I only raised my hand for questions I was certain about. In terms of marks, that approach was not a bad one. But what I did not understand stayed not understood.
After I started working, that view changed. When I was given a new job, I went about it carefully, checking over and over so as never to fail once. I made a detailed plan and wrote out every problem that seemed likely to arise. But the result was not as good as I had hoped. Of the problems I had written out, two actually happened, and most of the problems that happened were ones I had not written.
The colleague at the next desk, who joined when I did, was different from me. She tried things as soon as she thought of them, and changed her approach the moment she saw it was not working. She built something small, showed it to people, and fixed what they told her the same day. She failed far more often than I did, but in the end she produced a good result.
Where did that difference lie? I thought of failure as something to avoid; she thought of it as something to find early. Trying to avoid it means trying fewer things. And if you do not try things, you cannot even tell what you do not understand. In the end, what I had been doing was going on being safely wrong at my desk.
I have changed how I work a little since. First I break the work into pieces small enough that a failure can be recovered from. Within a piece that size, when in doubt I choose to try it. I keep a short record of what I tried and read it back just once a week. If I have tripped twice for the same reason, I take that to be a problem with my method rather than with luck.
Of course it is not that anything may be tried. Where people's safety, or money that cannot be got back, is involved, checking comes first. What matters is telling first which of the two situations you are in.
What matters is not the number of failures but what you learn from them and how quickly you put it to use, and that was when I first realised it. Even now, being wrong is not a pleasant thing. But the time the embarrassment lasts has grown much shorter than it used to be.

en: It has become normal for what you order to arrive the next day. Fast delivery is welcome, but it seems to me something has been lost because of it. With no time before getting it, the feeling after getting it is somehow thinner too. I have no intention of giving up convenience. p.e: When I was put in charge of training a new member of staff, I tried to teach everything thoroughly.

So I changed my approach.

p.e: When a question came I stopped answering at once, and asked back what he would do.

きにくるようになった。

r: たったころ、こんなことがあった。
p.e: Around a year in, this happened.

en:
When I was put in charge of training a new member of staff, I tried to teach everything thoroughly. I prepared a sheet setting out the steps in detail, and told him to come and ask any time there was something he did not understand. He listened readily and got through the work accurately, one item at a time. For the first few months it looked as though it was going well.
But around six months in, something started to bother me. In any situation the sheet did not cover, he would come to a halt. Even for things he could probably have worked out with a moment's thought, the first move was to come and ask what he should do. When I answered, he did exactly that. Accurate, but with no trace anywhere of a judgement of his own.
The cause lay not with him but on my side. In trying to make the time he spent not knowing as short as possible, I had taken away the chance to think along with it. Time spent not knowing is certainly not pleasant. But there are things that grow only inside that time.
So I changed my approach. When a question came I stopped answering at once, and asked back what he would do. At first he looked troubled, but before long he began coming to ask with his own view attached, saying he thought it was probably this. Sometimes he was wrong, but on those occasions his understanding after the explanation was deeper.
Around a year in, this happened. On a day I was off, a customer got in touch with a sudden change. It was a situation written nowhere on the sheet. He checked with the departments concerned himself, drew up two options, and went back to the customer with them. The report I received the next day differed slightly from the option I would have chosen. And his was probably the better one.
Of course it is not that one should wait over everything. Anything touching on safety, and anything fixed by the rules, I pass on accurately at the outset. Waiting is only for situations where the answer is not settled in advance. To leave someone alone without drawing that distinction is not bringing them on but abandoning them.
I had thought that teaching meant handing over answers. But what really ought to be handed over is the power to start moving where there is no answer. For that, the one teaching has to wait a little. Waiting is far harder than teaching.

q.q: 半年ほどたったころ、筆者は何が気になったのか。

p.e: A

B
Working from home has a problem that is hard to see.
It is that the boundary between work and life disappears.
When your desk is also where you eat, work carries on in your head even after you close the screen.

en:
A. Since I have been able to work from home, commuting time has disappeared. I can spend that time with my family or resting, and physically it is easier. At the office I was often interrupted mid-task, which does not happen at home. With more time to concentrate, I feel I now finish the same work in less time. There are of course moments when it is harder to consult someone, but that can be handled by being thoughtful about how you keep in touch.
B. Working from home has a problem that is hard to see: the boundary between work and life disappears. When your desk is also where you eat, closing the screen does not stop work carrying on in your head. Commuting is a nuisance, but I realised only after losing it that those minutes served to switch my mind over. Also, because nobody can see that you are struggling, time can pass with you carrying it alone.

r: くしようとするとき、まず
p.e: When we set out to improve something, the first thing we do is try to measure it in numbers.
Sales, head counts, marks.

r: ったかがはっきりする。
p.e: Put into numbers, whether a thing has risen or fallen is clear.
Discussion moves faster too.
So measuring by numbers is not in itself a bad thing.
The problem is that only what is easy to measure survives.
A library once ran an effort to increase the number of books lent out.
A target was set, and everyone checked the monthly figure.
After six months the number had indeed risen.
But when I spoke to the staff, their faces were not bright.
The number had gone up, they said, but something they had valued had gone down.
At that library the staff took time to hear out people looking for a book, and sometimes talked at length with people who went home without borrowing a single volume.
That time does not show up in the figures.

r: をすすめるようになり、
p.e: As they chased the lending figure they began recommending books likely to be borrowed on the spot, and the long conversations were pushed to the back.
Something similar happens in schools.
Exam marks can be measured; the wish to know more that is left behind after learning something cannot.
Ways to raise marks come to mind by the handful in a short time.
Ways to grow that wish do not come to mind readily.
When it comes to choosing which to do first, the side that comes to mind is the side that tends to be chosen.
This is not a matter of anyone being at fault.
A number has a shape you can explain to other people.
In a meeting, an argument without numbers is weak.
So it is always the person trying to protect what cannot be measured who carries the burden of explaining.

r: みがないわけではない。
p.e: It is not that what cannot be measured has no weight.

r: べることができないだけである。
p.e: It simply cannot be set beside a number and compared.
And yet, if judgements go on being made by looking only at what can be compared, what cannot be compared quietly disappears.

r: では、どうすればよいのか。
p.e: So what should be done?
One answer would be to make sure that a meeting held to look at numbers always hears one thing that is not a number.
That library, I gather, made a space at the end of the monthly report for one line about a conversation with a user that a member of staff remembered.
Simply having that line beneath the figures changed the direction of the discussion a little.
I am not saying do not measure in numbers.
I am saying that we should remember, from time to time, what lies outside the number we measured.

en:
When we set out to improve something, the first thing we do is try to measure it in numbers. Sales, head counts, marks. Put into numbers, whether a thing has risen or fallen is clear. Discussion moves faster too. So measuring by numbers is not in itself a bad thing.
The problem is that only what is easy to measure survives.
A library once ran an effort to increase the number of books lent out. A target was set, and everyone checked the monthly figure. After six months the number had indeed risen. But when I spoke to the staff, their faces were not bright. The number had gone up, they said, but something they had valued had gone down.
At that library the staff took time to hear out people looking for a book, and sometimes talked at length with people who went home without borrowing a single volume. That time does not show up in the figures. As they chased the lending figure they began recommending books likely to be borrowed on the spot, and the long conversations were pushed to the back.
Something similar happens in schools. Exam marks can be measured; the wish to know more that is left behind after learning something cannot. Ways to raise marks come to mind by the handful in a short time. Ways to grow that wish do not come to mind readily. When it comes to choosing which to do first, the side that comes to mind is the side that tends to be chosen.
This is not a matter of anyone being at fault. A number has a shape you can explain to other people. In a meeting, an argument without numbers is weak. So it is always the person trying to protect what cannot be measured who carries the burden of explaining.
It is not that what cannot be measured has no weight. It simply cannot be set beside a number and compared. And yet, if judgements go on being made by looking only at what can be compared, what cannot be compared quietly disappears.
So what should be done? One answer would be to make sure that a meeting held to look at numbers always hears one thing that is not a number. That library, I gather, made a space at the end of the monthly report for one line about a conversation with a user that a member of staff remembered. Simply having that line beneath the figures changed the direction of the discussion a little.
I am not saying do not measure in numbers. I am saying that we should remember, from time to time, what lies outside the number we measured.

p.e: People often say “ordinary is fine.”

r: いというだけでは、それが
p.e: Yet being common alone does not make something right, or make it suit you.

r: ①ここにおとしあながある。
p.e: Here is the pitfall.
You think you are aiming at ordinary, when in fact you are aiming at being the same as other people.
Sameness is reassuring, but reassurance and satisfaction are different things.
The word ordinary has another sense.
It means not forcing yourself.
That ordinary is worth aiming at.

r: をしていないかどうか。

en:
People often say “ordinary is fine.” But what is ordinary?
Ordinary is most often used to mean that many people do it that way. Yet being common alone does not make something right, or make it suit you.
Here is the pitfall. You think you are aiming at ordinary, when in fact you are aiming at being the same as other people. Sameness is reassuring, but reassurance and satisfaction are different things.

p.e: Email is fast.
You write when it occurs to you and send it at once, and the other person can read it whenever suits them.
It is a useful tool.
Does that mean letters are no longer needed?

r: ないのかというと、そうではないと
p.e: I do not think so.

r: えればはじめからやり
p.e: You choose the paper, take out the pen, and start again from the beginning if you make a mistake.
Even when you have finished, it does not arrive at once.
During that interval, the writer goes on thinking about the person.
The receiver senses it too.
When they open the envelope, they are receiving the time spent on it along with the words.

r: えたいことはメールで
p.e: Anything you want to convey quickly can go by email.
But when what you want to convey is the very fact that you spent time, nothing yet matches a letter.

en:
Email is fast. You write when it occurs to you and send it at once, and the other person can read it whenever suits them. It is a useful tool.
Does that mean letters are no longer needed? I do not think so. A letter contains time that email does not.
You choose the paper, take out the pen, and start again from the beginning if you make a mistake. Even when you have finished, it does not arrive at once. During that interval, the writer goes on thinking about the person.
The receiver senses it too. When they open the envelope, they are receiving the time spent on it along with the words.
Anything you want to convey quickly can go by email. But when what you want to convey is the very fact that you spent time, nothing yet matches a letter.

ti: 図書館は何を置くべきか

p.e: A.

But if you have to wait half a year to borrow the book you want, fewer people will come to the library at all.
Surely getting them through the door comes first.
Someone who starts visiting because of a popular book may in time reach for a volume at the back of the shelves.

r: くすることは、けっしてむだではない。
p.e: Widening the entrance is by no means wasted effort.
B.
Line up many copies of the same book and you cannot buy other books with that money.
Popular books can be had in bookshops, and wait a little and your turn comes round anyway.
What only a library can hold is the book that does not sell but is needed.

r: らすことより、ほかのどこにもない
p.e: The role of a public library lies, I think, in keeping the one volume that exists nowhere else, rather than in reducing the number of people waiting.

en:

Widening the entrance is by no means wasted effort.

What only a library can hold is the book that does not sell but is needed. The role of a public library lies, I think, in keeping the one volume that exists nowhere else, rather than in reducing the number of people waiting.

p.e: My grandfather was a man who mended anything that broke.
If a chair leg wobbled he looked underneath; if a clock stopped he opened the back.
If a bag handle gave way he would find thread of the same colour and put it back as it was.

r: どものわたしには、それがふしぎな
p.e: To me as a child it looked like a mysterious power.
Having grown up and become able to mend a few things myself, I have understood something.

r: っていたわけではない。
p.e: It was not that my grandfather had any special skill.

r: うかどうかがちがっていたのだ。
p.e: What was different was simply whether, faced with something broken, his first thought was that it might be mendable.
Only once you have thought that do you feel like looking inside.

r: ゆるんでいるだけ、という
p.e: And when you look, it is not rare for it to be no more than one loose screw.

r: わたしたちは、こわれたものを
p.e: When we see something broken, the first thing we do is look up the price of a new one.
We pass by the existence of mending it before the thought arrives.
That difference is not one of skill but one of order.
The thought that buying new is quicker is right in most cases.

r: が、だんだんなくなっていく。
p.e: And precisely because it is right, the chances to try the other way slowly disappear.
I once mended my grandfather's chair myself.
I opened the toolbox, looked underneath, and simply turning the wooden screws again stopped the wobble.
It took about ten minutes.
I still use that chair, and every time I sit on it I remember those ten minutes.
Had I bought a new chair, nothing would have been left to remember.
Of course, some things cannot be mended.
It is often cheaper to buy than to mend.

r: られていないものは、どうしようもない。
p.e: Where the parts are no longer made, there is nothing to be done.
Even so, I look inside once.
Whether you have that habit changes how you get on with the things around you a great deal.

r: らないのかもしれない。
p.e: This question of order may not be limited to objects.
A way of working that is not running well, or a relationship that has gone awry, also looks as though replacing it would settle the matter.

r: けれども、どこがゆるんでいるのかを
p.e: But looking first at where something has worked loose is sometimes quicker in the end.
My grandfather's toolbox is in my room now.
There is nothing special in it.
What was in it, I now think, was the habit of opening things up.

en:
My grandfather was a man who mended anything that broke. If a chair leg wobbled he looked underneath; if a clock stopped he opened the back. If a bag handle gave way he would find thread of the same colour and put it back as it was. To me as a child it looked like a mysterious power.
Having grown up and become able to mend a few things myself, I have understood something. It was not that my grandfather had any special skill. What was different was simply whether, faced with something broken, his first thought was that it might be mendable. Only once you have thought that do you feel like looking inside. And when you look, it is not rare for it to be no more than one loose screw.
When we see something broken, the first thing we do is look up the price of a new one. We pass by the existence of mending it before the thought arrives. That difference is not one of skill but one of order. The thought that buying new is quicker is right in most cases. And precisely because it is right, the chances to try the other way slowly disappear.
I once mended my grandfather's chair myself. I opened the toolbox, looked underneath, and simply turning the wooden screws again stopped the wobble. It took about ten minutes. I still use that chair, and every time I sit on it I remember those ten minutes. Had I bought a new chair, nothing would have been left to remember.
Of course, some things cannot be mended. It is often cheaper to buy than to mend. Where the parts are no longer made, there is nothing to be done. Even so, I look inside once. Whether you have that habit changes how you get on with the things around you a great deal.
This question of order may not be limited to objects. A way of working that is not running well, or a relationship that has gone awry, also looks as though replacing it would settle the matter. But looking first at where something has worked loose is sometimes quicker in the end.
My grandfather's toolbox is in my room now. There is nothing special in it. What was in it, I now think, was the habit of opening things up.

Take a photo, hurry to the next place.
What I could recall afterwards was only the route from station to station.

p.e: Since then I decide on one destination and leave the rest undecided.
What to do with the time left over I leave to the mood and the weather of the day.
Oddly enough, I remember more from the trips with less planned.

Before a trip I used to enjoy writing out all the places I wanted to go. I would mark a map, look up how long each journey took, and build a schedule from morning to night. I even thought the time spent planning was the best part.

Since then I decide on one destination and leave the rest undecided. What to do with the time left over I leave to the mood and the weather of the day. Oddly enough, I remember more from the trips with less planned.

en:
When someone is going to be late for a meeting, they sometimes say “I'll be there in five minutes.” In fact it often takes fifteen.
The person running late wants to believe they will arrive soon, and that hope comes out of their mouth as a number.
What matters to the person waiting is not a small number but an accurate one. If it is going to take fifteen minutes, being told fifteen at the outset means they can read a book or deal with something else.

en:
Even if you decide to start saving, trying to save what is left over usually does not last, because at the end of the month there is usually nothing left over.
People who manage it do it the other way round. On payday they move a set amount into another account first. They then live on what remains — and oddly, it turns out to be enough.
Rather than relying on willpower to keep it up, building the arrangement at the start is in the end easier.

When I grew up and started working, it looked different. Rather than fighting over the same piece of work, there were many situations where dividing it by what each person was good at produced a better result. At first this change confused me.
Thinking it over, competition had not disappeared. The opponent had changed. Instead of deciding who wins against the person beside you, you compete with things that are hard to see — last year's self, a deadline, the market.
The competition of running hard and coming first, and the competition of joining forces to finish by a deadline. Both require effort, but the kind of strength needed is, I now think, quite different.

p.e: My mother hardly ever looks at a cookbook.

Because the failures remain rather than vanishing, she does not stumble in the same place.

People who keep at something are strong, I think, less because they kept at it for long than because of how many times they corrected course while doing so.

p.e: When I was a student I belonged to the drama club.
I joined wanting to act, but I was stiff and my voice did not carry, and in my first year I was moved backstage.
To be honest, it stung.
I thought that whatever you did where the audience could not see, nobody would remember it.
What I was put in charge of was the lighting.
Which lights to bring down, and by how much, in which scene: you read the script closely and decide.
At first I simply moved my hands as instructed.
Following the table written by whoever had the job the year before, I read off a number and turned a dial.

r: それだけなら、だれがやっても
p.e: If that was all it was, I felt, it would come out the same whoever did it.
What changed it was the day I tried holding the lights a second longer in one scene.
The time the actor stands there saying nothing becomes slightly longer.
That alone changed the air in the house.
The sound of the audience catching its breath reached me, back behind the set.
Same script, same actor, same audience; the only thing changed was one second.
That was when I first understood.
It is not only the actors who make the stage.
The lights, the sound, the raising and lowering of the curtain.
Every one of them changes the way the watcher's mind moves.
The audience's eyes are on the actors, but the scene in front of those eyes is made jointly by the people behind.
After that, the way I read a script changed.

There were days when I talked it over with an actor and redid the way the lights came down again and again.
After the run ended, one of the actors told me that in that scene the lighting had helped him.
For someone on the side that is not used to being praised, a remark like that stays a long time.
I graduated and moved into other work, but this experience has stayed with me.
In any place there are those who stand at the front and those who hold it up out of sight.

r: めてしまうことがある。

The order the papers are put in for a meeting, or how bright a shop's entrance is, must be the same.
Whether a thing stands out and whether it is doing the work are two different matters.

p.e: Everyone has wished at some point that the other person would understand without being told.

en:
Everyone has wished at some point that the other person would understand without being told. But you cannot see inside another person's mind.
To read someone is to imagine, from how they seem, what they may be feeling, not to guess it correctly. Once you have imagined it, it is better to check in words, just to be sure.
If you are afraid to check and say nothing, the other person ends up feeling that they are not thought to matter.

p.e: At the end of autumn, in a corner of the garden, a single spider was making a white sack.

Even when a flock of birds comes to the garden, the white sack is lost against the colour of the leaves and goes unfound.

r: がいなくなってからも
p.e: A preparation made in order to protect goes on working after the one who made it is gone.

en:
At the end of autumn, in a corner of the garden, a single spider was making a white sack. Inside it are eggs.
The spider tied the sack firmly to a branch with its silk so that not even the wind would bring it down, and then went off somewhere. The parent does not live through the winter. Only the eggs are kept quietly, as though asleep, until spring.
Even when a flock of birds comes to the garden, the white sack is lost against the colour of the leaves and goes unfound. A preparation made in order to protect goes on working after the one who made it is gone.

q.q: 筆者がこの文章で言いたいことは何か。

鳥はくもの卵を見つけるのがうまい
親がいなくなっても、その備えは働き続ける

p.e: When you are practising something, there comes a point where you suddenly stop feeling any improvement.

r: ちたわけではないのに、
p.e: It is not that your ability has fallen, yet you end up in a state of going round and round the same spot.
This is where most people want to change their method.
They buy a book with a new way of teaching, look for a different teacher, and start again from the first chapter.

r: えたとたんに、それまで
にたまっていたものが、
わってしまうことがある。
p.e: But the moment you change, what had been accumulating in the body until then can end up never being used.

r: がすすめたいのは、やり
p.e: What I would recommend is to keep a record before changing your method.
Write just one line about what you managed today.
Keep that up for a month, and a difference of degree you had not noticed yourself appears on the paper.
Research says that people judge their own rate of progress to be lower than it is.

r: がらなくなっただけのことが
p.e: Feeling that you have stopped is, more often than not, simply progress having grown small enough not to rise into awareness.
A record puts that small progress into visible form, and joins it up with your next preparation.

en:
When you are practising something, there comes a point where you suddenly stop feeling any improvement. It is not that your ability has fallen, yet you end up in a state of going round and round the same spot.
This is where most people want to change their method. They buy a book with a new way of teaching, look for a different teacher, and start again from the first chapter. But the moment you change, what had been accumulating in the body until then can end up never being used.
What I would recommend is to keep a record before changing your method. Write just one line about what you managed today. Keep that up for a month, and a difference of degree you had not noticed yourself appears on the paper.
Research says that people judge their own rate of progress to be lower than it is. Feeling that you have stopped is, more often than not, simply progress having grown small enough not to rise into awareness. A record puts that small progress into visible form, and joins it up with your next preparation.

q.q: 筆者によると、上達が止まったと感じるのはなぜか。
o: 能力が落ちたから
進み方が小さくなって気づきにくくなったから
やり方が自分に合っていないから
練習の時間が足りないから
q.w: 「進み方が小さくなって、意識に上がらなくなっただけのことが多い」とあります。「能力が落ちたわけではない」とも述べています。

q.q: 筆者がすすめているのは何か。
o: 新しい先生を探すこと
最初の章からやり直すこと
できたことを記録すること
しばらく練習を休むこと
q.w: 「やり方を変えるより先に、記録を取ることだ」とあります。

p.e: Resting tends to be thought of as doing nothing.
But there are days when you have lain down all day and by evening your body feels heavier instead.

r: きをやめていないからだという。
p.e: This is said to be because the brain has not stopped working.
It seems that if too little comes in from outside, the human brain becomes unsettled.
You sleep better at night after a day of moving your arms and legs a little and getting a few light errands out of the way.
The older you get, the larger this difference becomes.

r: くのがつらくなって、さらに
p.e: Bones and muscles weaken quickly when they are not used, and once they weaken, moving becomes hard, so they are used even less.
Rather than stopping completely, make a day on which you move at half your usual speed.
That is what a day of rest means to me.

en:
Resting tends to be thought of as doing nothing. But there are days when you have lain down all day and by evening your body feels heavier instead.
This is said to be because the brain has not stopped working. It seems that if too little comes in from outside, the human brain becomes unsettled. You sleep better at night after a day of moving your arms and legs a little and getting a few light errands out of the way.
The older you get, the larger this difference becomes. Bones and muscles weaken quickly when they are not used, and once they weaken, moving becomes hard, so they are used even less.
Rather than stopping completely, make a day on which you move at half your usual speed. That is what a day of rest means to me.

寝る時間が長すぎたから
年齢が上がったから

p.e: Tidying the living room at home, I turned up as many as six cloth bags of much the same kind.
Every one had been kept on the grounds that I would use it one day.
But I had completely forgotten that there were six.
A possession you do not remember is no different from one you do not own.
There is a limit to the number of things a person can keep track of in their head.
Whatever goes beyond that number merely exists in the house, which amounts to not existing at all.
My father, after he retired, said something when he cut his clothes by half.
He had always been a man who cared about how he dressed, so this surprised me.
"When you have fewer, each one starts to seem like a treasure."

r: らすのは、がまんすることではなく、
えるようにすることなのだろう。
p.e: Reducing your belongings is probably not a matter of going without, but of making what you keep visible.

r: んだままにしておくより、
p.e: Using a small number of things every day is far more enjoyable than leaving sashes and clothes stowed at the bottom of a box.

en:
Tidying the living room at home, I turned up as many as six cloth bags of much the same kind. Every one had been kept on the grounds that I would use it one day. But I had completely forgotten that there were six.
A possession you do not remember is no different from one you do not own. There is a limit to the number of things a person can keep track of in their head. Whatever goes beyond that number merely exists in the house, which amounts to not existing at all.
My father, after he retired, said something when he cut his clothes by half. He had always been a man who cared about how he dressed, so this surprised me. "When you have fewer, each one starts to seem like a treasure."
Reducing your belongings is probably not a matter of going without, but of making what you keep visible. Using a small number of things every day is far more enjoyable than leaving sashes and clothes stowed at the bottom of a box.

p.e: A.
When a student makes a mistake, I correct it on the spot.
If they go on with the mistake uncorrected, it takes shape and stays.
I confine the correction to the answer, though.
I avoid any wording that denies the person's way of thinking.
It is less like cancelling something out than like bending it halfway to change its direction.
B.
Even when I notice a mistake, I let the student finish.
Stop them partway and you lose track of where they went off.
After hearing it all, I say "this far is right," showing the correct part first.
The student then often finds the mistake themselves.
Growth afterwards is faster when they have found it themselves.
What I fear most is their motivation being scattered.

en:
A. When a student makes a mistake, I correct it on the spot. If they go on with the mistake uncorrected, it takes shape and stays. I confine the correction to the answer, though. I avoid any wording that denies the person's way of thinking. It is less like cancelling something out than like bending it halfway to change its direction.
B. Even when I notice a mistake, I let the student finish. Stop them partway and you lose track of where they went off. After hearing it all, I say "this far is right," showing the correct part first. The student then often finds the mistake themselves. Growth afterwards is faster when they have found it themselves. p.e: Last autumn I walked around a small village at the end of a railway line.
It was because the village had been described in a book my friend's name appears on as author.

r: はどうなっているのかを
p.e: The photographs in the book were from about thirty years ago, and I wanted to see what it was like now.
Coming out of the station, fields and a wood opened out at once, with forest and mountains in the distance.
The road ran down towards the river, with an old wooden bridge partway along.

r: くなるまでかわいていて、
p.e: The planks of the bridge had dried until they were white, and they gave a low sound as I walked.
At the centre of the village stood a temple, and beside it a small shrine hall.
In front of the hall lay flowers made of Japanese paper.
Who had put them there I could not tell, but the colours had not faded, so they were clearly recent.
What surprised me was not how old the buildings were.
It was that the way of keeping the old form was not the same formula everywhere.

p.e: One house uses its original walls as they are.
Another has rebuilt the same form out of new materials.
Yet another has left only the side visible from outside as it was, and changed the inside to suit life today.
The three houses stand side by side, and from a little way off you cannot tell them apart.

r: すことじゃないんです。」
p.e: "Keeping something is not the same as capturing it in a photograph."
"Once the people living here are gone, what good is the form on its own?"
His own house was the third of the three.
When he had the kitchen done, he said, the one thing he kept was the old door.

"It is only what comes into view that I leave as it was."

p.e: Put like that, he was right.
An old town looks beautiful because life carries on in it, not because the old form is beautiful in itself.
The village has half the people it had thirty years ago.
There are houses where the young have come back, but many that stand empty.
Of the shops in the book, only one is still there.
Even so, every house still standing has been kept up, and nothing feels abandoned.
As I left the village, looking down at the water from the bridge, fallen leaves were drifting past.
This bridge too will be made new one day.

en:
Last autumn I walked around a small village at the end of a railway line. It was because the village had been described in a book my friend's name appears on as author. The photographs in the book were from about thirty years ago, and I wanted to see what it was like now.
Coming out of the station, fields and a wood opened out at once, with forest and mountains in the distance. The road ran down towards the river, with an old wooden bridge partway along. The planks of the bridge had dried until they were white, and they gave a low sound as I walked. At the centre of the village stood a temple, and beside it a small shrine hall. In front of the hall lay flowers made of Japanese paper. Who had put them there I could not tell, but the colours had not faded, so they were clearly recent.
What surprised me was not how old the buildings were. It was that the way of keeping the old form was not the same formula everywhere. One house uses its original walls as they are. Another has rebuilt the same form out of new materials. Yet another has left only the side visible from outside as it was, and changed the inside to suit life today. The three houses stand side by side, and from a little way off you cannot tell them apart.
It is not a question of which is right, a villager told me. "Keeping something is not the same as capturing it in a photograph." "Once the people living here are gone, what good is the form on its own?" His own house was the third of the three. When he had the kitchen done, he said, the one thing he kept was the old door. "The parts you touch every day may as well be made new." "It is only what comes into view that I leave as it was." Put like that, he was right. An old town looks beautiful because life carries on in it, not because the old form is beautiful in itself.
The village has half the people it had thirty years ago. There are houses where the young have come back, but many that stand empty. Of the shops in the book, only one is still there. Even so, every house still standing has been kept up, and nothing feels abandoned.
As I left the village, looking down at the water from the bridge, fallen leaves were drifting past. This bridge too will be made new one day. Even so, I thought, if this village goes on being a village, that will count as having kept it.

p.e: It is because you start to feel you have to give them something.

When we try to help someone, we tend to put something in between. Speaking through words borrowed from books or other people is safe, but it does not reach the other person. A borrowed word carries no weight of its own, so it cannot take the weight of the person in front of you. It is precisely when you are asked for advice that you should not hurry to an answer.
Listening to someone is probably not a matter of having an answer ready, but of being ready to spend a stretch of time together in which there is no answer. Perhaps the power to listen is decided by whether you can hold a stretch of time without exchanging words. Being unable to stay silent and blurting out "in that case" is not for the other person's sake but because you yourself are uneasy. That becomes possible, I think, only when you are not trying to change the other person.
These days, when someone comes to me, I check one thing at the start. Whether they want an answer, or simply want to talk. If they say they want an answer, I answer as plainly as I can. In the evenings, people from the neighbourhood talk amiably on the walkway. Safety, or a life with the water in view. Make it a matter of choosing one of the two and no answer comes. Looking for a form that satisfies both a little seems to work better, anywhere in the world.
The river water still cannot be drunk. Even so, being a town with the water in view matters to me.

r: めたあと、そのかばんを

r: はそのかばんについて

r: まっていったのである。

ti: 土を使わない野菜作り

p.e: A way of growing vegetables without soil is spreading.
It is a method in which the roots are kept in water with the necessary substances mixed into it.
Because it is done indoors, the quantity does not change even in a year of bad weather.
Insects are less of a problem, so less chemical is used as well.

r: いことばかりのように
p.e: It looks like nothing but advantages, but there are problems.
First, it uses a lot of electricity.
It is because the light and the warmth are made by machine.
In a field outdoors, sun and wind are free.

r: だめになることもある。
p.e: And if the machinery stops, the whole crop can be lost in a day.
Second, the range of what can be grown is limited.
Vegetables whose leaves are eaten suit it, but those that grow underground, and those that are kept a long time, are difficult.
This method is not growing because of taste or price.
What counts is being able to put the growing close to the town.
Carrying produce in from a distant field costs both time and money, and freshness is lost on the way.
Grow it on the floor above the shop and leaves picked in the morning can be sold the same day.
There is a view that the shortness of the journey makes up for the electricity.
Which is right cannot yet be said.

r: がなくなるわけでもないだろう。
p.e: Nor are field vegetables likely to disappear.

r: わっていくのかもしれない。
p.e: But the idea that vegetables come from soil may change little by little.
Plenty of people already buy in the shop without minding which way it was grown.
Thought of as more to choose from, that is not a bad thing.

en:
A way of growing vegetables without soil is spreading. It is a method in which the roots are kept in water with the necessary substances mixed into it. Because it is done indoors, the quantity does not change even in a year of bad weather. Insects are less of a problem, so less chemical is used as well.
It looks like nothing but advantages, but there are problems. First, it uses a lot of electricity. It is because the light and the warmth are made by machine. In a field outdoors, sun and wind are free. And if the machinery stops, the whole crop can be lost in a day. Second, the range of what can be grown is limited. Vegetables whose leaves are eaten suit it, but those that grow underground, and those that are kept a long time, are difficult.
This method is not growing because of taste or price. What counts is being able to put the growing close to the town. Carrying produce in from a distant field costs both time and money, and freshness is lost on the way. Grow it on the floor above the shop and leaves picked in the morning can be sold the same day. There is a view that the shortness of the journey makes up for the electricity.
Which is right cannot yet be said. Nor are field vegetables likely to disappear. But the idea that vegetables come from soil may change little by little. Plenty of people already buy in the shop without minding which way it was grown. Thought of as more to choose from, that is not a bad thing.

p.e: I like looking at old maps.
Lay out maps of the same town in order of date and your eye goes not to what has been added but to what has gone.
The river has narrowed, a road that curved has been straightened, a small pond has disappeared.
A map does not put down everything that is on the ground.
The paper has its limits, and everything on it would make it unreadable.
So the maker always selects.

r: とすということである。
p.e: To select is to leave out.
What gets left out is decided by what the map was made for.
A map for people on foot and a map for cars keep different things.
A road map has no need of narrow lanes.
A walker's map has no need of motorway exits.
The same ground takes a different visible shape according to what it is to be used for.

r: とされたものが、やがて
p.e: What troubles me is that what gets left out eventually disappears from the ground as well.
A path not on the map comes to be used less.
A path that is not used stops being kept up.
A path that is not kept up vanishes into the grass within a few decades.
The narrow sloping lane I walked as a child is not on the current map either.

r: していたはずなのに、いつの
p.e: The map was supposed to be a copy of the ground, and yet somewhere along the way the map has come to decide the ground.
On one city's old map there was a point marked as a watering place for horses.
On the current map there is nothing.
Going there, I found a small open space with a single stone set in it.
Nothing was written on the stone.
Asking someone nearby, all that remained was the account that water had once come up there.
The name nobody remembers any more.
Once the name goes, the place becomes a place that is nothing in particular.
And a place that is nothing in particular is the first to be chosen when something is next to be built.
Of course this is not a demand that everything old be kept.
Many people have surely been helped by a road being straightened, and there are schools built on filled-in ponds.
Stop the rebuilding and a town becomes hard to live in.
But when something is erased, a record can be left in a form that shows it was erased.
Most maps now live inside a screen.
Unlike paper, they have no limit of space.
They can select what to show while holding on to everything they hold.

r: られるようにしている
p.e: Some cities have made their old maps available to look at at any time.
So in terms of what is technically possible, a map could already be made without leaving anything out.

r: がいなかっただけのことだと
p.e: What has not been kept, I think, simply had nobody who decided to keep it.

p.e: Look at the trunk of a felled tree and you can see circles laid one inside another.

So there is a limit to what can be read from a single trunk.
Many are gathered and compared, and whether the same pattern appears is checked.
It is because with one tree alone, that tree's own circumstances cannot be told apart from the weather.
A tree goes on writing down its surroundings using its own body.

p.e: Keep at a sport long enough and the days you lose outnumber the days you win.

p.e: What makes it possible to carry on even so is that there are things you understand after losing.

I corrected the shape of my step, checked my jumping height, counted my arm swings.
My opponent's striking was ferocious, and merely taking it left the shock in my arms.
There were days I stayed bent over and could not get up.
And still I lost to the same opponent the next time.

r: すようになってからだ。

It was not that my opponent was the stronger.

He was waiting there for it, and taking the timing from me.
Your own habit is invisible to you.
What you cannot see does not get corrected however often you repeat it.
From then on I made a rule of not moving my body on a day I lost.
Instead I recall the day's movements and write them out.
Written out, the moments where I wavered and the moments where I was settled come apart and become visible.
The moments where I wavered usually have the same shape.
Correcting that shape works far better than piling up the same practice.
Even with less time spent using my body, I began to win.
Taking pride on a day you win is easy.

r: らずにいるのはやさしくない。
p.e: Holding neither your opponent nor yourself in contempt on a day you lose is hard.

ti: 作品に説明を付けるべきか

p.e: A
In an art gallery there is sometimes a long explanation beside a painting.
I think it is unnecessary.
The words get in before you have seen what is painted with your own eyes.
What sort of person the maker was, what they had in mind in making it.
Look after learning that and you see it exactly as you were told.
The more valuable the work, the longer the explanation gets.
To look at art is, I think, the time you spend standing there not understanding.
That time must not be taken away from anyone.
There is a painting I stood in front of for a long time as a child without even knowing what it was.
I still remember not understanding it.
I would like the explanation put after the looking.
B

r: ってしまえばいい、という
p.e: Some people say the explanation beside a painting should simply be removed.

r: っていられるのは、ある
p.e: But only someone with a certain amount of practice can stand there knowing nothing.

What matters is the amount and the placing.
Put a single short line in front of the painting and the detail somewhere else.
One line is enough to stop the feet.
And someone who has stopped begins to look for themselves.
The time of standing without understanding comes only to those who got through the door.

p.e: On the hill in the town where I live there is a small shrine.

r: ふたがしてあって、のぞくことはできない。
p.e: It is covered, so you cannot look in.

In the morning, when the sun comes through the trees, the well cover alone is lit.

Last autumn part of the steps collapsed.
It was the day the water rose and the embankment below gave way.
The question became who would see to a shrine that could no longer be reached.
It does not belong to the city, nor to a temple.

A meeting was held and I went.
The atmosphere was heavy at first.
The discussion ran in all directions.
Some said everyone should contribute to the cost.

p.e: Others said it was wrong for people who never use it to pay.

Deciding it that way, I think, is what did the trick.
